reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A recurrent deletion of the distal 1q21.1 interval generated by non-allelic homologous recombination between flanking segmental duplications, distinct from the proximal TAR-associated region
Highly variable phenotype including microcephaly, developmental delay and mild to moderate intellectual disability
Increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and of schizophrenia
Congenital heart disease and cataracts occur in a proportion of cases
The reciprocal duplication of the same interval tends to produce mirror-image features such as macrocephaly and is also associated with autism
Penetrance is incomplete and expressivity variable, so the deletion may be inherited from an apparently unaffected parent
Some carriers show no discernible clinical effect, complicating interpretation and counselling
Chromosomal microarray is the first-line diagnostic test
reference.pathophysiology: The distal 1q21.1 region is flanked by segmental duplications that misalign during meiosis and predispose to non-allelic homologous recombination, generating a recurrent deletion or its reciprocal duplication. The interval contains dosage-sensitive genes influencing brain growth and neuronal connectivity, and their altered dosage underlies the neurodevelopmental phenotype and the mirror-image head-size effects of deletion (microcephaly) versus duplication (macrocephaly). Marked incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity indicate that additional genetic background and possibly a second genetic hit strongly modify the outcome.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombocytopenia-absent radius (TAR) syndrome from the proximal 1q21.1 region
Other recurrent copy-number syndromes causing developmental delay and psychiatric risk
Primary schizophrenia without a copy-number change
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as first-line to detect and size the deletion and distinguish it from the proximal TAR region
FISH or MLPA to confirm the finding
Parental studies to establish inheritance and counsel recurrence risk
Echocardiography to screen for congenital heart disease
Developmental, autism and (in later life) psychiatric evaluation
redFlags: Emerging psychotic symptoms in adolescence or adulthood
Visual impairment from cataract requiring ophthalmology input
reference.prognosis: Because penetrance is incomplete, the range of outcomes is broad, from unaffected carriers to individuals with intellectual disability, autism or psychiatric illness. Overall prognosis depends on the presence and severity of congenital heart disease, the degree of neurodevelopmental involvement and later psychiatric health.
pitfalls: Confusing the distal 1q21.1 deletion with the proximal TAR-region deletion, which has a different phenotype
Counselling an inherited deletion as benign because the transmitting parent appears unaffected
Failing to screen for congenital heart disease and cataract
Overlooking the elevated psychiatric risk in long-term follow-up
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
